When a release tag is supplied, the local annotated tag exists and peels to a concrete source commit.

ML-KEM-768 keygen and encaps NIST ACVP vectors match the checked-in KAT header constants.
ML-KEM-1024 keygen and encaps NIST ACVP vectors match the checked-in KAT header constants.

The benchmark CSV has the expected schema, required rows, positive numeric fields, and bounded PQCP/baseline timing ratios.
The benchmark_provenance.json sidecar cryptographically binds to the benchmark CSV bytes.
The benchmark CSV contains valid ML-KEM rows for every configured parameter set with positive cycles and time values.
The benchmark CSV contains valid ML-DSA rows for every configured parameter set with positive cycles and time values.
The benchmark export includes additive min, median, p90, p99, max, MAD, and sample-count rows for every supported ML-KEM and ML-DSA parameter set without changing the legacy metric contract.
Every configured cost-of-assurance guardrail metric was evaluated and passed.
A local release bundle manifest exists and hashes the extracted release notes for the selected version.
Release evidence claims are bound to captured release-check stdout transcripts with recorded SHA-256 hashes.

The ACVP serial harness rejects malformed inputs (bad hex, unknown commands, wrong sizes, oversize payloads) with the documented ERROR:* responses, as exercised by ztest_acvp_serial and bound to acvp_negative_scenarios.json.

The ACVP serial readline timeout fires under stalled-frame conditions, emits ERROR:TIMEOUT, and recovers cleanly for the next command (proven by ztest_acvp_serial::test_readline_timeout in the captured ACVP serial transcript).

Every replay-eligible case from scripts/acvp_negative_scenarios.json is exercised directly through pqcp_acvp_process_command() by tests/ztest_acvp_serial_negative and produces the documented ERROR:* response on the wire.

ML-KEM-specific negative paths (INVALID_LEVEL for unsupported levels, WRONG_SIZE for truncated/oversize encaps and decaps payloads, INVALID_HEX for non-hex encaps payloads) are rejected with the documented ERROR:* responses by tests/ztest_acvp_serial_negative.

ML-DSA-specific negative paths (WRONG_SIZE for short SIGN payload, INVALID_HEX for non-hex SIGN payload, WRONG_SIZE for truncated VERIFY payload, INVALID_CMD for too-many VERIFY fields) are rejected with the documented ERROR:* responses by tests/ztest_acvp_serial_negative.
scripts/acvp_negative_scenario_floor.json locks every compatibility-floor negative scenario so malformed ACVP cases cannot be removed, renamed, duplicated, or weakened without a release-gate failure.
Every sanitizer-enabled native_sim ztest run captured by scripts/run_sanitizer_checks.py finished without an AddressSanitizer error report.
Every sanitizer-enabled native_sim ztest run captured by scripts/run_sanitizer_checks.py finished without an UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer runtime error report.

When CONFIG_PQCP_KAT_BOOT_VERIFY=y is set, the SYS_INIT(APPLICATION) hook in src/crypto/kat_boot_verify.c runs a deterministic keygen/encaps/decaps for every enabled ML-KEM level and keygen/sign/verify for every enabled ML-DSA level, and the system reaches ztest main without calling k_panic(). Proven by tests/ztest_kat_boot_verify on qemu_x86_64.

ML-KEM-512/768/1024 decapsulation, each run 32 times against a valid and 32 times against a deliberately corrupted ciphertext, produces median cycle counts whose relative variance stays under a documented bound. This is a runtime smoke test, not a constant-time proof; the assurance documentation (docs/assurance-model.md, docs/publications.md) states the same caveats. Proven by tests/ztest_ct_smoke on qemu_x86_64.

The built ML-KEM decapsulation code path is scanned for variable-latency division instructions associated with KyberSlash-class regressions. This is static regression evidence, not a formal side-channel proof.

The release pack includes an unsigned in-toto Statement-style PQC assurance attestation binding release evidence artifact hashes to the ledger metadata.
The release pack includes a verified PQC asset trace map linking cryptographic assets to source files, Kconfig symbols, assurance claims, ztests, transcript markers, and CBOM components.

The partner-review PQC assurance policy evaluated the ledger, CBOM, attestation, and release metadata and passed without failures.

The release pack exports the assurance digest into a generated C header and verifies that samples/pqcp_assurance_status can compile it into firmware.

The release pack includes a migration-readiness report derived from the assurance profile, evidence quality result, and CBOM profile properties.

The firmware deployment evidence chain emitted by samples/pqcp_deployment_advisor on qemu_x86_64 (verdict, seal, and assurance passport markers) replays bit-for-bit on the host: scripts/run_evidence_chain_replay.py captures the live device transcript, compiles the UNMODIFIED firmware replay-verifier C (src/evidence/deployment_evidence_verdict_replay.c, src/evidence/deployment_evidence_seal_replay.c, src/evidence/deployment_assurance_passport_replay.c) into tools/evidence_verifier, recomputes every terminal digest, and requires the verdict-to-seal and seal-to-passport digest bindings to hold. Proven by the captured step transcript containing the device markers and the host verifier's CHAIN OK verdict.

Every transcript-facing evidence parser (the firmware verdict, seal, assurance-passport, tamper-matrix, and evidence-trail replay-verifier line parsers compiled unmodified for host, plus the ML-DSA signature chunk reassembler) and every host-portable fleet wire parser (the deterministic CBOR validator and map/array readers in src/experimental/fleet/fleet_cbor_map.c, COSE_Sign1 and protected-header decode/verify in src/experimental/fleet/fleet_cose_sign1.c, COSE_Key decode in src/experimental/fleet/fleet_cose_key.c, and the policy bytecode module codec with its structural verifier and VM in src/experimental/fleet/fleet_policy_codec.c, src/experimental/fleet/fleet_policy_verify.c and src/experimental/fleet/fleet_policy_vm.c, also compiled unmodified for host) survive a deterministic mutational fuzz campaign driven by scripts/run_fuzz_checks.py and tools/evidence_fuzzer under ASan+UBSan with -fno-sanitize-recover=all: multiple seeded campaigns over corpus lines from real captured device transcripts and over binary seeds produced by the real encoders complete with zero memory errors or undefined behavior. The fleet targets additionally assert invariants on every input, handed to the parser in an exact-size heap buffer: whatever the decoder accepts re-encodes byte-for-byte (decode(encode(x)) round trip), rejected inputs leave outputs unused (zeroed, untouched, or bounded by the input), and a policy module that passes the structural verifier may only fault in the VM for data-dependent reasons and always fails closed. Proven by the captured step transcript containing one PQCP_FUZZ PASS marker per seed, each reporting targets>=10 (6 text replay parsers plus the 4 fleet CBOR, COSE_Sign1, COSE_Key and policy-codec targets), and a PQCP_FUZZ BINARY_ACCEPTED line showing every binary parser accepted inputs. The campaign is coverage-guided: the target parsers are compiled with SanitizerCoverage edge instrumentation, any mutated input that reaches a never-before-seen edge is promoted into the in-memory corpus, and the PQCP_FUZZ PASS marker records edges_covered, edge_guards, and the number of evolved corpus entries. Evolution is deterministic for a fixed seed and build; the harness and the mldsa backend are deliberately uninstrumented so coverage pressure stays on the parsers under test. The channel frame codecs are not fuzz targets: they need a fake Zephyr kernel header and PSA-backed runtime helpers, a larger host shim than this harness allows itself.

Under the pqcp_ct_insn QEMU TCG plugin (tools/tcg_ct_plugin), every ML-KEM-768 decapsulation in tests/ztest_ct_instr executes the identical number of guest instructions AND the identical number of guest memory accesses (loads and stores counted separately) for a valid ciphertext and for a corrupted (implicit-rejection) ciphertext: scripts/run_ct_instruction_checks.py brackets each decapsulation between two marker addresses resolved from the ELF symbol table, the plugin counts guest instructions and data memory operations between the markers, and the runner requires exact (insns, loads, stores) tuple equality across all valid and corrupted regions. This proves control flow and memory-operation counts are input-independent at guest granularity; which addresses are accessed and microarchitectural timing remain out of scope, and the project does not claim a formal constant-time proof.

Every src/*.c module is assigned a measured evidence level by scripts/audit_evidence_coverage.py: L0 untested (no ztest suite references a function the module defines), L1 tested, L2 gated (an exercising suite is wired into extended checks, release_check, or a workflow), L3 claimed (also bound by the claim catalog or asset trace map). A call-graph pass separates modules that are only reached through another tested module from modules unreachable from every test. The audit is a ratchet against scripts/evidence_coverage_baseline.json: the release gate fails if any module's level drops or if a NEW module appears with no test. The claim states measured coverage, not completeness: modules recorded as L0 in the baseline are known-unproven and stay visible in the transcript summary.

The host appraisal of firmware-emitted evidence is a registered, verifier-bound, post-quantum-countersigned Attestation Result. scripts/run_transparent_appraisal.py builds tools/evidence_verifier (pqcp-evidence-verify) and tools/evidence_register, replays the committed device transcripts (signed fixture included), and emits for each a deterministic CBOR statement binding the passport digest, the device ML-DSA public key hash, the evidence trail head, the verdict (CHAIN OK or REJECT), the SHA-256 of the verifier binary that produced it, and the SHA-256 of the transcript. Statements are appended to an RFC 9162 Merkle log built from the unmodified firmware transparency code (include/pqcp_zephyr/fleet_transparency.h, src/fleet_transparency_*.c), whose checkpoints are signed with ML-DSA-65 (vendored mldsa-native, FIPS 204 deterministic variant). Inclusion receipts and release-to-release consistency proofs are re-verified offline against a pinned log key, and the receipt's statement is re-checked against a fresh replay of the supplied transcript. Two independently written verifiers check the Merkle math: the single-source C and scripts/rfc9162_reference.py (stdlib only, no shared code); the driver runs both on every case and requires accept/reject agreement. It then requires every forgery in a fixed list to be REJECTED by the C verifier with the expected reason (bit flips in statement, path node, leaf index, tree size, checkpoint root and signature; wrong log key; an older signed checkpoint with a newer claimed size; a receipt proof from a forked tree under a valid checkpoint; a registered forged verdict and a statement from another verifier build; a tampered transcript; equivocation by two validly signed checkpoints of one log; history rewrite; rollback and replayed checkpoints; truncated, trailing-byte and non-canonical CBOR; seeded random bit sweeps), plus one positive control per class so a verifier that rejects everything cannot pass. Python cannot verify ML-DSA, so for signature-byte flips the C verifier must reject while python reports the signature as delegated; those cases are excluded from the differential count. Proven by the captured step transcript containing PQCP_APPRAISAL_RECEIPT PASS with consistency=ok, differential_agree=169/169, forgeries_rejected=156/156 and controls=11/11. Not claimed: the demo log key is generated from a public seed and is not production custody; there is no witness cosigning or quorum, and the log is single-operator, so a log that equivocates is detected only by a party that holds two of its checkpoints; the verifier binary hash identifies the verifier, it does not prove the verifier correct.

Four edge firmware state machines (the principal directory in src/edge/edge_identity_directory.c, the session registry in src/edge/edge_session_registry.c, the credential cache in src/edge/edge_credential_cache.c and the policy distributor in src/edge/edge_policy_distributor.c) conform to small abstract security models under seeded stateful property testing. tests/ztest_edge_model runs on qemu_x86_64 against the real in-image modules: for each module it drives seeded random operation traces (at most 64 operations; at least 64 seeds per module is required by this claim), checks the model's safety properties after every operation (a quarantined principal is never observed as healthy and a re-register never lifts a quarantine; session slots and per-principal quotas never leak and a double close changes nothing; a revoked credential is never authorized again, is never overwritten and its slot is never recycled; the active policy epoch never regresses through a stale promote or a rollback and the distributor audit stays clean; identifier counters start at 1), and uses each module's own _audit() function as a second oracle. A violation is shrunk on the device by delta debugging to a 1-minimal trace and printed as a replayable PQCP_MODEL_COUNTEREXAMPLE marker. The measure of the models' power is rediscovery of known defects: scripts/run_model_checks.py --rediscover re-injects, one at a time into a private copy of the sources, the edge defects that were found by hand and fixed in b7d4cc1 (revoked-credential slot recycling, put over a revoked credential, quarantine lifted by re-register, by observe and by tick, session close double decrement, session slot leak, stale policy promote, rollback rewriting a digest-covered field, first identifier off by one), rebuilds, and counts a defect as rediscovered only when the run prints a COUNTEREXAMPLE naming the module the defect lives in. Proven by the captured step transcript containing one PASS PQCP_MODEL_CHECK marker per module with at least 64 seeds, a PQCP_MODEL_SUMMARY with modules=4 and violations=0 whose totals equal the per-module sums, no COUNTEREXAMPLE marker in the unmutated run, and a PQCP_MODEL_REDISCOVERY PASS marker whose rediscovered count is at least the ratcheted baseline in scripts/model_rediscovery_baseline.json, whose defect count has not shrunk, and whose per-defect PQCP_MODEL_DEFECT lines agree with the marker; every defect that is not rediscovered carries a written allowance and is counted in the marker. Not claimed: traces are bounded; the models are abstract safety properties, not full functional specifications; only the edge modules above are covered; rediscovering known bug classes shows sensitivity to those classes, not the absence of other defects; there is no concurrency, so mutex interleavings are not explored; a failing counterexample must be replayed as a hand-written ztest before it is treated as a firmware defect.

Under the pqcp_ct_trace QEMU TCG plugin (tools/tcg_ct_plugin), every ML-KEM-768 decapsulation of tests/ztest_ct_trace on the deployed qemu_x86_64 image leaves an identical fingerprint on four observation channels at three optimisation levels (Zephyr default -Os, speed -O2, debug -Og) for all ciphertexts of one key (a valid one and corruptions at different positions): the sequence of executed instruction addresses, the exact data addresses, the data addresses at 64-byte cache-line granularity, and the dividend of every x86 div/idiv (variable-latency operations, decoded from opcode bytes). The detector's power is measured, not assumed: scripts/ct_leak_rediscovery.py re-injects five known PQC timing-leak patterns (a secret-dependent branch in the clangover style, a secret-indexed table lookup, a KyberSlash-style division, an early-exit ciphertext comparison and a secret-dependent early continue) into a private copy of mlkem-native, rebuilds the image and requires the trace test to report a divergence for each, while three harmless changes (a dead volatile store, a public-constant branch and a constant-time multiplication rewrite) must NOT be flagged. The same run records which leaks the earlier counts-only evidence (security.ct_instruction_count) would have missed. This is relational leakage testing of an emulated x86_64 image on sampled keys and ciphertexts: not a constant-time proof, no microarchitecture, no ARM Cortex-M timing, and variation across different keys (public-matrix rejection sampling) is reported but not judged.

An exhaustive emulated single-instruction fault campaign (scripts/run_fault_campaign.py, scripts/fault_inject.py, scripts/fault_oracle.py) patches a copy of the deployed qemu_x86_64 image of tests/ztest_fault_oracle at every instruction of the mlkem-native ML-KEM-768 decapsulation and mldsa-native ML-DSA-65 verify code (and the PQCP wrappers) with two fault models (instruction skip; branch/cmov/setcc inversion), runs each variant under QEMU and classifies the observations by cryptographic meaning: KEM_FO_BYPASS (a corrupted ciphertext yields the genuine shared secret) and SIG_VERIFY_BYPASS (a tampered signature or message is accepted) are the exploitable classes. Results are only trusted after calibration: three unfaulted runs must be identical and valid, and identity patches must all be NO_EFFECT. The gate measures the countermeasure rather than assuming it: on the image whose power-on self-test has only valid-only vectors the campaign must still find exploitable sites (the campaign is sensitive), and with CONFIG_PQCP_KAT_BOOT_VERIFY_NEGATIVE (a corrupted ciphertext must not yield the genuine key; a tampered signature and a different message must be rejected) the number of exploitable sites must be zero and boot-time detections must exceed the valid-only image's. Permanent single faults on x86_64 under emulation only: no hardware fault physics, no multi-fault or data bit-flip models, callees such as Keccak and NTT are outside the target set, no key recovery, and a boot self-test does not defend against faults injected after boot.

Extending the emulated fault campaign (claim security.fault_campaign_boot_selftest) with fault TIMING, the deployed qemu_x86_64 image is measured against two fault timings: permanent faults that appear after the boot self-test has run (the patch is written through the QEMU gdbstub at an arm point, because the SDK plugin API v4 cannot write guest state) and single-shot transient faults (the patch is applied once on the first execution of a site in the scenarios of a corrupted ciphertext or tampered signature, the instruction is stepped, and the original bytes are restored). Every instruction of the mlkem-native ML-KEM-768 decapsulation and mldsa-native ML-DSA-65 verify code is faulted with two models (instruction skip, branch inversion); verdicts are cryptographic (a corrupted ciphertext yielding the genuine key, a tampered signature accepted); campaigns are only trusted after identical golden runs, identity-patch controls and zero injection errors. Two opt-in wrapper countermeasures are evaluated: CONFIG_PQCP_FAULT_CANARY (after each operation the same backend function rejects a stored negative input) and CONFIG_PQCP_FAULT_DUPLICATE (two runs must agree). The release gate re-measures the four cells the claim rests on and requires: the base image (boot self-test with negative vectors only) shows exploitable sites under BOTH timings (the campaign is sensitive), and the image with both countermeasures shows none under either timing. The full measured ablation, published in docs/fault-campaign.md, is: base 9 exploitable post-boot / 9 transient; canary only 0 / 8 (a transient fault hits only the real operation); duplicate only 9 / 0 (a permanent fault corrupts both runs identically); both 0 / 0. Single faults on x86_64 under emulation only: the transient model faults the first execution of each site, no multi-fault attacks (two faults can defeat the compare itself), no hardware fault physics, callees such as Keccak and NTT are outside the target set, the results depend on this build's code layout and compiler, and the countermeasures cost about one extra operation per call each plus about 8 KB of RAM for the canary.

Signing with rejection loops legitimately leaks, through timing, the outcome of its accept/reject decisions, so a whole-signature trace comparison cannot be applied. The ML-DSA-65 signing of tests/ztest_ct_trace_mldsa on the deployed qemu_x86_64 image is therefore tested relationally modulo declassification: mldsa-native's own upstream MLD_CT_TESTING_DECLASSIFY annotations (routed through a shim valgrind header, with no change to the vendored library) become trace-segment boundaries for the pqcp_ct_trace TCG plugin, and two signing runs that agree on every declassified value so far must execute the next segment identically on four channels (executed instruction addresses, exact data addresses, 64-byte cache lines, div/idiv dividends) and reach the same next declassification site. The input family holds rho, K, tr, the message and the hedging randomness fixed and varies only the secret components s1, s2 and t0, so the first commitment and challenge coincide and the segments are comparable; runs differ in iteration count (12 to 43 declassification events per signature), which a whole-trace comparison could not tolerate. Clean at three optimisation levels with zero violations over a majority of all segments. The detector's power is measured: scripts/ct_leak_rediscovery_mldsa.py re-injects four leak patterns on the secret-handling path of signing (a secret-dependent branch, a secret-indexed table lookup, a KyberSlash-style division, a secret-dependent early continue) into a private copy of mldsa-native and requires each to be reported, while three harmless changes (a dead volatile store, a public-constant branch, a public-index branch) must not be flagged, and it records which leaks a totals-only check would have missed. Segments that follow a declassification of a large buffer (the challenge, w0/w1, the signature) are processed as public data and are compared only when their declassified inputs coincide. The crafted secret keys are not valid key pairs. This is relational leakage testing of an emulated x86_64 image on sampled inputs against the upstream declassification policy, not a constant-time proof; no microarchitecture and no ARM Cortex-M timing.

The deployed ML-KEM-768 image built for the Cortex-M3 board mps2/an385 (Thumb-2 code from the Zephyr SDK's arm-zephyr-eabi GCC, run under QEMU 10.0.2) is tested for operand-dependent latency, a channel the x86_64 trace test cannot see: the pqcp_ct_trace TCG plugin decodes every Thumb-2 UDIV, SDIV, UMULL, SMULL, UMLAL and SMLAL executed during decapsulation and records, per instruction address, the exact operands, their bit lengths and the documented Cortex-M3 long-multiply predicate (both operands below 65536, ARM DDI 0337). Decapsulation of one key must present identical streams for the valid ciphertext and every corrupted one on the model that applies to each instruction: a division fails on any bit-length variation, a long multiply on any change of the documented predicate, and any site that runs a different number of times fails; the address-level channels (instruction addresses, exact data addresses, 64-byte lines) must also be identical. The run is clean at three optimisation levels. The conservative reading is kept as a ratcheted inventory rather than hidden: sites whose exact operands vary with the secret while the documented model is constant (BearSSL measured Cortex-M3 devices deviating from the documented long-multiply rule) are counted, and the count may not grow beyond the committed baseline scripts/ct_vlat_inventory_baseline.json. The detector's power is measured by scripts/ct_leak_rediscovery_m3.py, which re-injects into a private copy of mlkem-native a UDIV and an SDIV by a runtime divisor of a decrypted coefficient and a UMULL whose operand magnitude follows a decrypted message bit, requires all three to be reported, requires three harmless variants (a UDIV on public loop operands, a UMULL of a secret coefficient by a small constant, a dead store) not to be flagged, and records how many leaks the address-level channels alone would have missed. This is operand recording under emulation on sampled inputs against a documented latency model; no cycle-accurate model, no hardware measurement, no other Cortex-M core (a Cortex-M4 or M33 has single-cycle long multiplies and shares the divider rule) and not a constant-time proof.

ML-DSA-65 signing is tested on two Cortex-M cores with the declassification-aware relational test of claim security.ct_trace_declassified, extended with the operand-latency channels of claim security.ct_trace_cortex_m_latency: the same tests/ztest_ct_trace_mldsa image is built for mps2/an385 (Cortex-M3) and mps2/an386 (Cortex-M4) and run under qemu-system-arm with the pqcp_ct_trace plugin, which now cuts each signing at the upstream MLD_CT_TESTING_DECLASSIFY events on 32-bit ARM and fingerprints, per segment, the bit lengths of every UDIV/SDIV operand and the documented long-multiply predicate (both operands below 65536) of every UMULL/SMULL/UMLAL/SMLAL. Two segments that agree on every declassified value so far must match on instruction addresses, exact data addresses, 64-byte cache lines and the core's latency model: an M3 long multiply terminates early on operand size (ARM DDI 0337) and so is a channel, an M4 long multiply is single-cycle and is not; both share the variable-latency divider. Measured: on the Cortex-M4 model signing is clean (zero violations over 546 comparable of 600 segments) at three optimisation levels; on the Cortex-M3 model the address channels and the divider are clean but the long-multiply predicate varies with the secret in the Montgomery and NTT arithmetic (8, 12 and 4 instruction sites at -Os, -O2 and -Og, inventoried by site and ratcheted so the count may only shrink against scripts/ct_vlat_signing_baseline.json). The release gate requires the M4 run clean, the M3 run to show no violation on any channel other than the long multiply and at least one such finding (a positive control showing the core distinction is live), and the site counts not to exceed the baseline. This documents a core-selection finding, not a defect proof: it follows ARM's documented early-termination rule, which BearSSL measured real M3 devices to deviate from, under emulation with recorded operands, no cycle model, sampled inputs and crafted non-valid keys. Not a constant-time proof.

The Cortex-M3 long-multiply finding of claim security.ct_trace_cortex_m_signing is closed by a mitigation that is itself verified by the same test: scripts/mldsa_fixed_latency.py patches a private copy of mldsa-native (the vendored tree is never edited) so that every signed 32x32-to-64 product in the Montgomery and NTT arithmetic is built from four 16x16 partial products computed with the 32-bit MUL instruction (single-cycle on Cortex-M3/M4, constant-time on every Cortex-M), plus shifts and adds, instead of SMULL. Three things are checked at three optimisation levels on the mps2/an385 image under QEMU: the patched build shows no violation and no attributed variable-latency site on any Cortex-M3 channel over at least 400 comparable segments; the stock build still shows the long-multiply finding at the same run (a positive control, so a clean patched result cannot come from a dead detector); and both builds produce the same FNV-1a digest over every signature of the run, so the patch changes neither the output nor, with the segment relation, the control flow. The helper is separately checked against native 64-bit multiplication on edge values and 20 million random pairs under UBSan. The cost is recorded, not hidden: the instruction overhead of a whole signing is measured from the trace and ratcheted against scripts/ct_vlat_mitigation_baseline.json. This is verification under emulation against the documented Cortex-M3 latency model with recorded operands: no cycle count (only instruction counts), no hardware measurement, other arithmetic that is not a multiply (rounding, hint, sampling) is covered by the same trace test only for the sampled inputs, the mitigation is opt-in and not part of the default build, and it is not a constant-time proof.

The Cortex-M3 operand-latency verdicts of claims security.ct_trace_cortex_m_latency, security.ct_trace_cortex_m_signing and security.ct_trace_cortex_m_mitigation are re-evaluated under a second latency model on the very same traces: the pqcp_ct_trace plugin records, per instruction site and per declassification segment, a hash of the CMEmu latency class (ct_latency_models.h: long multiplies by which 16-bit halves of each operand are non-zero and, for signed forms, signs; divides by a cycle formula; CMEmu is a cycle-exact Cortex-M3 r2p1 model derived from timing measurements, MSWiM 2025, re-implemented here from its published description with no CMEmu code), next to the documented ARM DDI 0337 model, and the analysis reports a per-site disagreement matrix (PQCP_CT_TRACE_LATENCY_MODELS). Hypotheses were registered before the measurement in docs/ct-latency-model-sensitivity.md. Measured at three optimisation levels: the models agree on every stock ML-DSA-65 signing site (8, 12 and 4); the claim-15 fixed-latency patch has no failing site and no segment violation under the CMEmu model either; and the two models disagree on exactly one ML-KEM-768 decapsulation site, the UMULL of the multiply-and-shift that replaced the division after KyberSlash (mlk_poly_compress_d10_c), constant under the documented rule and one cycle faster for a zero operand under CMEmu. The release gate requires the C and Python classifiers to agree on at least 100000 operand cases, the stock ML-DSA signing image to show CMEmu-failing sites (the second channel is live), the patched image to have zero failing sites and zero violations under CMEmu at every level, and the ML-KEM CMEmu-only site count not to exceed the committed baseline scripts/ct_vlat_models_baseline.json (it may only shrink). This is a measurement of how much verdicts depend on the latency model, not an exploit: a one-cycle difference under one chip revision's third-party measurements, not validated against silicon here, possibly hidden by flash wait states and pipeline effects; the two classifiers share one source of rules; no cycle-accurate execution; sampled inputs. Not a constant-time proof.

The one ML-KEM-768 decapsulation site that only the CMEmu latency model flags (claim security.ct_trace_cortex_m_latency_models: the UMULL of (uint64_t)u * 2642263040 in mlk_scalar_compress_d10, one cycle faster for u == 0) is repaired by an operand offset and the repair is verified by the same instrument under both latency models. scripts/mlkem_fixed_latency.py patches a private copy of mlkem-native (the vendored tree is never edited) so the operand is u + 0x10001, whose two 16-bit halves are never zero, and the offset is removed from the 64-bit product afterwards (an empty asm statement stops the compiler folding it away): the value is unchanged and the latency class is constant. A host self-test checks all 3329 inputs of both functions for value equality with the original and that the stock operand has two CMEmu latency classes while the repaired one has exactly one (and one documented-model class). On the Cortex-M3 image under QEMU at all three parameter sets and three optimisation levels the release gate requires: the stock image still shows the CMEmu-only site (positive control); the repaired image has no failing site under the documented model and none under the CMEmu model; an FNV-1a digest over every shared secret of the run (including implicit-rejection outputs for corrupted ciphertexts) is identical in both builds; and the instruction overhead of a whole decapsulation stays under a committed ceiling (measured at most 0.03 percent, 0.06 percent and 0.12 percent at -Os, -O2 and -Og across the three parameter sets, against 34 to 75 percent for the full 16x16 split of claim 15). The modelled variable-latency cycle total of one decapsulation is also measured per key: the stock image's total differs between ciphertexts of one key by 1 to 2 cycles on more than 800 thousand instructions (relative amplitude near 1e-6), the repaired image's spread is exactly 0, and the gate requires a stock spread of at least 1, a repaired spread of 0 and a stock spread of at most 8 cycles and 1e-5 relative. This is verification under two latency models with recorded operands: the CMEmu rules are a third party's measurements of one chip revision and are not validated against silicon here, no cycle count (instruction counts only), one multiply site, the repair is opt-in and not part of the default build, and it is not a constant-time proof.

The number of attempts ML-DSA-65 signing needs does not depend on the secret key at a stated resolution. scripts/mldsa_rejection_study.py builds the real mldsa-native on the host (deterministic signing, a private copy that exports the attempt counter; the vendored tree is never edited), signs M random messages with each of K random keys, tests the per-key attempt histograms for homogeneity with a chi-square test (implemented without SciPy and checked against closed-form values) and correlates the per-key mean with the sum of absolute coefficients of s1, s2 and t0. Hypotheses were registered before the measurement in docs/ct-latency-model-sensitivity.md. Measured once at 200 keys by 5000 messages: pooled mean 5.144 attempts, chi-square 5481.9 on 5373 degrees of freedom (p = 0.147), the spread of per-key means (1.30 percent) equal to the sampling-noise expectation (about 1.27 percent), and no significant correlation with any key statistic. The release gate runs a reduced 60 keys by 3000 messages study and requires the self-test of the statistics to pass and the homogeneity test not to reject at p >= 0.001 (a regression guard: a vendor update that made the attempt count key-dependent would fail it). ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-87 were measured too (100 keys by 5000 messages each, p = 0.99 and p = 0.54). An exploratory positive correlation of the per-key mean with the sum of absolute t0 coefficients (r between 0.13 and 0.25 in the three parameter sets) was tested with a pre-registered one-sided test on fresh seeds (600 keys by 5000 messages): r = 0.092, p = 0.0121, not confirmed at the registered alpha of 0.01, and the s1 and s2 controls were null. This is a null result at a stated resolution, not a proof: a dependence below roughly 0.5 percent of the mean, or one specific to rare keys, would not be seen; ML-DSA-65 only; host build, not the Cortex-M image; random keys and messages, not adversarial ones; deterministic signing; no timing measurement.

The deployed ML-KEM-768 decapsulation and ML-DSA-65 signing images built for a Cortex-M33 (ARMv8-M, QEMU board mps2/an521/cpu0, Zephyr SDK GCC, QEMU 10.0.2) are tested with the pqcp_ct_trace TCG plugin on the M4-style channel set (instruction addresses, exact data addresses, 64-byte cache lines, divider latency; Cortex-M33 long multiplies are single-cycle and are not a channel): decapsulation shows no failing site at three optimisation levels (one candidate multiply site whose exact operands vary while the model is constant) and signing shows zero violations over at least 70 percent comparable segments of the declassification-aware relation at three optimisation levels, as on the Cortex-M4. Hypothesis H14 was registered before the run in docs/ct-latency-model-sensitivity.md. This uses the documented ARMv8-M latency rules only: no third-party measured model of the M33 was used, so the model comparison of security.ct_trace_cortex_m_latency_models does not extend to this core; QEMU with recorded operands, no cycle model, sampled inputs, ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 only; not a constant-time proof.

After ML-KEM-768 decapsulation, encapsulation and key generation and ML-DSA-65 signing and key generation return, the dead stack frames below the caller are measured on the Cortex-M4 image under QEMU and an opt-in stack wipe is verified. The pqcp_ct_trace plugin (option residue) records every stack word written during a traced region and reads it back at the end marker, and scripts/ct_residue_analysis.py counts the non-zero words and the words equal to the call's own shared secret (the output buffer excluded). Measured on the stock image: about 300 non-zero words after decapsulation, among them a complete 8 word copy of the shared secret in the Keccak permutation frames of every corrupted ciphertext run (no word of the stored secret key survives), and about 330 to 400 non-zero words after signing. CONFIG_PQCP_STACK_SCRUB (default off) makes the wrappers overwrite the stack below the caller with 32 bit stores. The release gate builds the stock and the scrubbed image at three optimisation levels for these five entry points and requires, for each, that the stock image leaves at least 100 non-zero words (and literal copies of the secret inputs or outputs for decapsulation at every level and for the other ML-KEM and key generation entry points at the default level, using a dictionary of the random bytes the call drew), that the scrubbed image keeps no shared secret word and less than half of the words, that the declassification aware leakage verdict of signing still holds with the wipe, and that the instruction overhead stays under a committed ceiling (measured about 1.3 to 2.2 percent for the ML-KEM entry points and 1.1 to 2.6 percent for the ML-DSA ones, with each wipe depth set from the deepest stack write measured on the image plus a margin). This is an emulated measurement: caches, DMA and other threads are not covered, the wipe depth is measured and not proven, the sampled inputs include crafted key variants that are not valid key pairs, the dictionary check cannot recognise Keccak lanes that mix the rejection seed with the ciphertext, and residue is not an exploit. Not a constant-time proof.

The SHA3 inside the ML-KEM library (the sha3_256 and sha3_512 exported by the single level ML-KEM-768 build) is compared with the SHA3 of Zephyr's crypto API, which Zephyr 4.5 backs with Mbed TLS behind the PSA layer and which shares no code with the library, on qemu_x86_64. The test hashes every input length from 0 to 300 bytes, which includes both sponge rate boundaries (136 bytes for SHA3-256, 72 bytes for SHA3-512), and 700 pseudo random longer lengths up to 1500 bytes, and requires every one of the 1001 digest pairs to be identical. A flipped input bit has to change both library digests, which shows the comparison is able to fail. The release gate requires at least 1000 lengths, zero mismatches, the control marker and a successful image run. This checks the hash functions the key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation use for matrix expansion, seeds and the key derivation, against an independent implementation, on one board and one build. It does not cover the SHAKE functions, other targets or inputs beyond 1500 bytes, and it is not a proof of correctness.
